# third_party/css — what this is, and what it is NOT

**This is a FORK of NetSurf LibCSS, not a vendor drop.** Twenty-three files
under `libcss/` carry LogitOS modifications, one of them (`src/parse/canon.c`,
5,425 lines) is first-party code living inside the vendored tree, and 26 commits
touch it. Nothing recorded that until this file existed, and the failure that
follows from not recording it is the one this repository warns about most: the
next person opens `src/select/properties/border_radius.c`, reads the NetSurf
copyright banner the surrounding files carry, and concludes it is upstream code
they must not touch.

## What is here

| directory | upstream |
|---|---|
| `libcss/` | NetSurf LibCSS |
| `libparserutils/` | NetSurf LibParserUtils |
| `libwapcaplet/` | NetSurf LibWapcaplet |

All three are MIT, and `make test-license-audit` gates that.

## The upstream revision is NOT recorded, and this file will not invent one

The vendoring commit is **`f840b45be` — "third_party/css: vendor NetSurf LibCSS,
trimmed to sources"**. It did not record the upstream revision it was taken
from, and guessing one here would be worse than saying so: a wrong revision
makes `git diff <base>` produce a diff nobody can trust, which is a slower and
more expensive way to be wrong than having no baseline at all.

To recover it, diff an unmodified file (one absent from the list below — e.g.
`src/lex/lex.c`) against upstream tags until it matches, then record the answer
**here**.

## The LogitOS surface, generated rather than remembered

```sh
grep -rl LogitOS third_party/css/libcss/src third_party/css/libcss/include | sort
```

That command is the authority; the list below is its output on 2026-08-29 and
will go stale the moment someone edits another file. Run the command.

```
include/libcss/canon.h                     include/libcss/computed.h
include/libcss/properties.h                include/libcss/select.h
src/bytecode/opcodes.h                     src/parse/canon.c
src/parse/important.c                      src/parse/language.c
src/parse/language.h                       src/parse/parse.c
src/parse/properties/border_radius.c       src/parse/properties/properties.c
src/parse/properties/properties.h          src/parse/propstrings.c
src/parse/propstrings.h                    src/select/computed.c
src/select/dispatch.c                      src/select/properties/border_radius.c
src/select/properties/height.c             src/select/properties/properties.h
src/select/select.c                        src/select/select_config.py
src/stylesheet.h
```

**Two of those are entirely first-party FILES, not patches**, and each says so
in its own first line rather than relying on this one:
`src/parse/properties/border_radius.c` and
`src/select/properties/border_radius.c`. `src/parse/canon.c` is a third.

## Two of the files above are GENERATOR INPUTS

`src/select/select_config.py` and `src/parse/properties/properties.gen` are
read by generators that emit checked-in sources:

- `src/select/select_generator.py` → `autogenerated_computed.h`,
  `autogenerated_propget.h`, `autogenerated_propset.h`,
  `autogenerated_destroy.inc`
- `src/parse/properties/css_property_parser_gen.c` → `src/parse/properties/autogen/*.c`

Both are **fixpoints against the checked-in tree**: regenerating reproduces it
byte for byte. `make check-cssgen` asserts the first one and is wired to
`ci-host:`. The failure it exists for is a hand edit inside a generated header
that the next regeneration silently reverts — the same shape
`tools/gen_as_opcodes.py --check` guards in `fsroot/as/lib/asc.as`.

**So a new simple property is two configuration lines, not two hundred of
boilerplate.** That is the reason this fork is affordable, and it is the thing
to check before deciding it is not.

## Rebasing

Assume we do not. The divergence is semantic, not textual: `@layer` /
`@supports` / `@container` are parsed as `CSS_RULE_MEDIA` with an `all` /
`not all` media list, `parsePseudo()` makes an unknown pseudo INERT instead of
invalid, `language.c` carries a weak hook out to
`c/apps/browser/css_extra.c`, and the property table has names upstream does
not have. Upstream will not take any of that.

What that costs, stated so nobody has to rediscover it: **we give up upstream's
maintenance of the part we depend on and did not write** — the cascade,
specificity, `!important`, the computed-value machinery, the ancestor bloom
filter and the content-hashed style arena. That is the expensive half of a CSS
engine and it is exactly the half this fork exists in order to keep.
